single-beam operation (synchrotron radiation and gamma-ray beams)
J/psi run beyond the standard parameters

summary.plain: The electron-positron collider at Italy's Frascati laboratory that began colliding beams in 1969, a ring 105 metres around at up to 3 GeV total energy. Its experiments found that electron-positron collisions make hadrons at a high rate and later joined the study of the J/psi. It shut down in 1993.

start.display: planned; the EIC's start of operations is not dated in the sources read (2032 is the 2023 expectation for the ePIC detector, which may have moved)

intervals.label: commissioning and first operation at design energy

summary.plain: A ring-shaped particle accelerator at Brookhaven National Laboratory, running since 1960. It once held the world speed record for protons and its experiments won three Nobel Prizes; today it accelerates particles before feeding them into other machines, including the RHIC collider.

The electron-positron collider at the Institute of High Energy Physics in Beijing, which first collided beams on 16 October 1988. Its detector, the Beijing Spectrometer (BES), measured the tau lepton mass and studied charm physics until 2004, when the machine was rebuilt as BEPCII.

intervals.label: approval of the BEPC Upgrade Project

summary.plain: The rebuilt two-ring electron-positron collider at the Institute of High Energy Physics in Beijing, running in the tau-charm energy region from 2008. It hosts the BESIII detector. Since July 2024 it has been undergoing an upgrade to higher energy and luminosity, which was in commissioning in 2026.
A proton accelerator at Berkeley, California, completed in 1954 and built with an energy just above what is needed to make an antiproton. In 1955 it did, and it ran until 1993.
A small ring, a quarter the size of the AGS, built in 1986-1991 to give protons and heavy ions a first push before they enter the AGS. It lifts protons from 200 million to 1.5 billion electronvolts.

The first machine in Brookhaven's proton chain: a 140-metre linear accelerator that has given hydrogen ions 200 million electronvolts since 1971, before they are passed to the Booster, the AGS and RHIC.

intervals.label: first beam delivered to an experimental hall
6 GeV era (until the 12 GeV Upgrade shutdown)
12 GeV Upgrade: 6 GeV operations ended, installation
12 GeV Upgrade: beam commissioning (first beams to Hall D, 7 May 2014)

beam_energy.display: 12 GeV (maximum; 11.6 GeV to Hall D in operation)

summary.plain: Jefferson Lab's main particle accelerator, which fires a continuous beam of electrons at nuclear targets in four experimental halls. It reached its 4 GeV design energy in 1995, was raised to 6 GeV in 2000, and was upgraded to 12 GeV between 2012 and 2016.

A proposed 100-kilometre electron-positron collider, designed as a Higgs factory and developed at the Institute of High Energy Physics in Beijing. It is to be hosted in China, but its site has not been selected, and it was left out of China's 2026-2030 five-year plan.

A ring at CERN that slows down antiprotons so scientists can trap them, make antihydrogen atoms and compare matter with antimatter. It started up in 2000 and paused with the rest of CERN’s injectors for a long upgrade shutdown in August 2026.

intervals.label: CLEO running ended; CESR continues as a light source

summary.plain: Cornell University's electron-positron storage ring, which first collided beams in 1979 at energies chosen to make the new bottom-quark Upsilon states. Its experiments CLEO and CUSB studied beauty and charm particles until 2008; the ring still feeds Cornell's X-ray source.

A proposed linear electron-positron collider designed as an addition to CERN's accelerator complex, to be built in three stages from 380 GeV up to 3 TeV. Its design is developed by an international collaboration of more than 70 institutes. It is not approved.
Brookhaven's first big accelerator: a ring that in 1953 became the first to send protons to billions of electron volts and the first to deliver a beam outside the machine. It closed in 1966.

An electron-positron collider at Italy's Frascati laboratory, tuned to 1.02 GeV so that collisions make phi mesons in large numbers (a phi factory). It hosted the KLOE and KLOE-2 experiments until 2018 and now runs SIDDHARTA-2, with first beams in 1997.

intervals.label: e+e- collider operation (DORIS, DORIS II, DORIS III)

summary.plain: DESY's first electron-positron collider, in Hamburg, running from 1974. It confirmed the charm quark's bound states, produced Upsilon mesons after its 1982 upgrade, and hosted ARGUS, which first saw B-meson mixing in 1987, and Crystal Ball.

The Electron-Ion Collider is a new particle collider being built at Brookhaven Lab, in partnership with Jefferson Lab, by adding an electron ring to the tunnel of the retired RHIC collider. It will collide polarised electrons with protons and nuclei to map the quarks and gluons inside them.

intervals.label: approved by CERN Council; construction and installation

summary.plain: A small 30-metre ring added to CERN’s antiproton machine. It slows antiprotons about fifty times more, so far more of them can be caught in the traps where antihydrogen is made. It paused for a long shutdown in August 2026.

A proposed 91-kilometre electron-positron collider in a new tunnel beneath the CERN area and neighbouring France and Switzerland, intended as a Higgs factory. The feasibility study was published in March 2025 and the 2026 European Strategy update recommends it; the CERN Council is to decide by 2028. It is not approved.

start.display: after the 2028-2029 long shutdown; LBNF beam to DUNE planned for 2031

summary.plain: A rapid-cycling ring 474 metres around that takes protons to 8 billion electronvolts. It feeds the Booster neutrino beam and the rest of the Fermilab chain.

end.display: between Run Ia (ended May 1993) and Run Ib (began December 1993)

summary.plain: The first machine in the Fermilab chain: it turns hydrogen ions into a 400-million-electronvolt beam and passes them to the next accelerator.

A 3.3-kilometre ring that accelerates protons to 120 billion electronvolts. Its beam makes the NuMI neutrinos and will make the LBNF beam for DUNE, but it has not operated since July 2024; a restart was planned for October 2026.

start.display: after the 2028-2029 long shutdown; LBNF beam to DUNE planned for 2031

summary.plain: A new 215-metre superconducting accelerator being built at Fermilab. It will replace the old first-stage machine and let the laboratory make the most intense high-energy neutrino beam in the world.

start.display: by late 2014 (first documented step: 6 batches stacked); not before the Tevatron stopped in 2011

summary.plain: A fixed-energy storage ring sitting in the same tunnel as the Main Injector. It stacks protons while the Main Injector accelerates, so the neutrino beam can be made faster.

intervals.label: First proton-antiproton collisions (engineering test run, 1.6 TeV)
1.8 TeV collider era (Run 0 in 1987 and 1988-89, Run I in 1992-96)

summary.plain: The proton-antiproton collider that was the most powerful in the world until the LHC. It ran at Fermilab until 2011 and was where the top quark was found.

intervals.label: HERA I at 820 GeV protons (first data in summer 1992)

injection_energy.display: 40 GeV (protons from PETRA); 12 GeV (electrons from PETRA)

summary.plain: A major upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider now being installed. By replacing about 1.2 kilometres of the ring with new magnets and equipment it will squeeze the beams harder so that many more collisions happen each second, giving the experiments roughly ten times more data.

intervals.label: Technical Design Report published; no site selected

summary.plain: A proposed linear electron-positron collider with a 500 GeV baseline design, extendable to 1 TeV. The 2013 design report named two candidate sites in Japan, Kitakami and Sefuri, and the Japanese community now promotes northern Japan. No site has been selected and the project is not approved.

The world's first machine to collide two beams of protons head-on, built at CERN and running from 1971 to 1984. It convinced physicists that colliding hadrons could work, and it held the record for collision rate among hadron colliders until 2004.
The first machine in the J-PARC chain: a 300-metre linear accelerator that gives hydrogen ions their initial energy before they are passed to the ring accelerators.

intervals.label: shutdown after the Great East Japan Earthquake
operation at 760 kW after the 2023 beamline upgrade

summary.plain: The largest J-PARC accelerator: a 1.6-kilometre ring that accelerates protons to 30 billion electronvolts and fires them at the target that makes the neutrino beam.

intervals.label: 181 MeV injection (before the Linac energy upgrade)

summary.plain: A fast-cycling ring that takes protons from the linac up to 3 billion electronvolts 25 times a second, feeding both a neutron source and the main ring.

The 600-metre linear accelerator at KEK that makes the electrons and positrons for the KEKB and SuperKEKB colliders. It has run since 1982 and today delivers 7 billion-electronvolt electrons and 4 billion-electronvolt positrons.

KEK's first big accelerator, a proton ring finished in 1976. From 1999 it produced the neutrino beam for K2K, the first experiment to send neutrinos hundreds of kilometres to a distant detector. Experiments ended in 2005.

intervals.label: shut down for the SuperKEKB upgrade

summary.plain: A three-kilometre-long machine at the KEK laboratory in Japan that smashed electrons into positrons at different energies from 1998 to 2010. It made huge numbers of B mesons for the Belle experiment and set a world record for collision rate.

A long particle accelerator at Los Alamos National Laboratory that fires protons at high energy. Originally built to study the strong nuclear force, it later produced the neutrino beam for the LSND experiment and today serves nuclear-security and materials research.
CERN’s first slow-antiproton ring, which ran from 1982 to 1996. It supplied the beams for the first antihydrogen atoms in 1995 and was later rebuilt as a different ring.

The largest electron-positron collider ever built: a 27-kilometre ring under the Swiss-French border that ran from 1989 to 2000 and produced about 17 million Z particles. Its tunnel was then reused for the Large Hadron Collider.

The world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator: a 27-kilometre ring of superconducting magnets under the Swiss-French border that steers two beams of protons in opposite directions and smashes them together inside four large experiments, including ATLAS.

The straight accelerator that started every proton used in CERN's experiments for forty years. It took protons up to 50 million electronvolts and passed them to the Proton Synchrotron Booster, and it was switched off for the last time in November 2018.

An 86-metre straight accelerator, 12 metres underground, that is the first step for every proton used at CERN. It accelerates hydrogen ions to 160 million electronvolts and has been the source of the beams that end up in the Large Hadron Collider since 2020.

intervals.label: MAMI operation (MAMI B 855 MeV, MAMI C about 1.5 GeV)

summary.plain: MAMI is the electron accelerator of Mainz University: a cascade of racetrack microtrons that produces high-precision electron beams up to 1.5 GeV, used to study the structure of the nucleon and of atomic nuclei.

MESA is a new electron accelerator being built at Mainz University that recovers most of the beam energy in superconducting cavities, giving a very intense electron beam of up to 155 MeV for precision experiments such as P2 and MAGIX.

NICA is JINR's new collider in Dubna for heavy ions and polarised protons and deuterons, built on the Nuclotron. Its first run began in March 2025 and circulated xenon beams in both rings; collisions at the MPD detector are the next goal.

beam_energy.display: up to 6 AGeV for light ions (Z/A ~ 0.5)

summary.plain: The Nuclotron is JINR's superconducting ring accelerator in Dubna, in operation since 1993. It supplies protons and ions up to gold at several GeV per nucleon to fixed-target experiments such as BM@N and injects the NICA collider.

SLAC's second electron-positron collider, a ring 2.2 kilometres around that ran from 1980 to 1990 at about 29 GeV. Detectors including MAC, the PEP-4 time projection chamber and Mark II studied quark jets, the tau lepton and electroweak effects. Its ring was reused for PEP-II.

injection_energy.display: 9.0 GeV e⁻ and 3.1 GeV e⁺ (full-energy injection from the linac)

summary.plain: A particle collider at SLAC that smashed together electrons and positrons at slightly different energies to produce large numbers of B mesons, studied by the BaBar detector from 1999 to 2008.

DESY's 2.3-kilometre electron-positron ring in Hamburg, which collided beams from 1978 to 1986. Experiments there (TASSO, MARK J, JADE, PLUTO, CELLO) found the first direct evidence of the gluon in three-jet events in 1979.

CERN's oldest working accelerator, a 628-metre ring that first accelerated protons in 1959. For a short time it was the most powerful accelerator in the world, and until it paused for Long Shutdown 3 on 31 August 2026 it fed every beam that ends up in the Large Hadron Collider.

Four small accelerator rings stacked on top of each other that take particles from the linear accelerator and give them their first big push before the Proton Synchrotron. Adding the Booster in 1972 let CERN put more than a hundred times as many protons into the next machine.

summary.plain: A giant underground ring at Brookhaven National Laboratory that collided beams of gold atomic nuclei and of protons with aligned spins at nearly the speed of light, recreating conditions from just after the Big Bang. It ran from 2000 to 2026 and is now being rebuilt into a new machine, the Electron-Ion Collider.

intervals.label: Super Charm-Tau factory project at BINP

cms_energy.display: 5 GeV (upper end of the 2 to 5 GeV design range)

summary.plain: A proposed electron-positron collider at the Budker Institute in Novosibirsk, Russia, for 2 to 5 GeV collisions with polarised electrons and a luminosity of about 10^35, built to study charm quarks and tau leptons. Only a preliminary 2018 design report exists; no approval or construction is recorded.

intervals.label: installation in the FAIR tunnels (first project stage)

summary.plain: SIS100 is the central new ring of the FAIR facility, a 1.1-kilometre superconducting accelerator in an underground tunnel that will accelerate ions of all elements to 99% of the speed of light. It is under construction, with beam commissioning planned for the second half of 2027.

intervals.label: commissioning of SIS18 and the ESR

summary.plain: SIS18 is GSI's 216-metre ring accelerator that boosts ions from every element up to about 90% of the speed of light. It feeds GSI's experiments and will serve as the injector for FAIR's new SIS100 ring.

SLAC's two-mile-long linear accelerator, which fires electrons (and, in its early years, positrons) down a straight underground tunnel. It has fed three generations of SLAC's experiments: the original fixed-target program, the SLC and PEP-II colliders, and today the LCLS X-ray laser.

A particle collider at SLAC that smashed together beams of electrons and positrons tuned to the mass of the Z boson, letting physicists study that particle's properties with the SLD detector from 1989 to 1998.

intervals.label: operating with the upgraded linac (1.3 GeV; power ramping toward 2.8 MW)

summary.plain: A powerful particle accelerator at Oak Ridge National Laboratory that fires pulses of protons into a liquid-mercury target to produce neutrons for research. The same process also produces a very pure, well-timed source of neutrinos used by experiments such as COHERENT.

intervals.label: dedicated synchrotron-radiation facility; collider operation ended

summary.plain: SLAC's first electron-positron collider, a single ring about 80 metres across that began running in 1972. At SPEAR, the Mark I experiment found the J/psi particle (1974), proving the charm quark, and the tau lepton (1975). Since 1990 it has run only as an X-ray source.

A seven-kilometre ring at CERN that has been the laboratory's workhorse since 1976. It accelerates protons to 450 billion electronvolts and hands them to the Large Hadron Collider, and in the 1980s it was rebuilt to collide protons with antiprotons, which is how the W and Z particles were discovered.

cms_energy.display: 7 GeV (upper end of the 2 to 7 GeV design range)

peak_luminosity.display: above 5 × 10^34 cm^-2 s^-1 (design goal at 4 GeV)

summary.plain: A proposed electron-positron collider for the tau-charm energy region, 2 to 7 GeV, planned for Hefei, China, with about 50 times the luminosity of BEPCII. Its accelerator design report appeared in 2025; approval in China's 2026-2030 plan is pending and its site within Hefei is not yet chosen.

specs.collision_scheme: nano-beam scheme with a large crossing angle at the interaction point

summary.plain: The rebuilt version of the KEKB collider in Japan. It squeezes its electron and positron beams down to nanometre thinness so they collide far more often than before, and since 2020 it has held the world record for collision rate.

accelerator:tristan.name: Tri Ring Intersecting STorage Accelerators in Nippon

summary.plain: KEK's 3-kilometre electron-positron collider in Tsukuba, Japan, which in November 1986 reached the world's highest collision energy of 50 GeV. Its three detectors AMY, TOPAZ and VENUS searched for the top quark and tested QCD from 1987 to 1995; the tunnel was then reused for KEKB.

The 24-metre electron-positron ring of the Budker Institute in Novosibirsk, Siberia, which replaced VEPP-2M. It collides round beams at up to 2 GeV and has served the CMD-3 and SND detectors since 2010; CMD-3 alone reports about one inverse femtobarn collected.

The electron-positron collider of the Budker Institute in Novosibirsk, Siberia, that ran from the 1970s to 2000 at energies up to 1.4 GeV. Its detectors OLYA, ND, CMD-2 and SND measured how electron-positron collisions make hadrons, the basis of modern low-energy data. It was rebuilt as VEPP-2000.

The high-energy electron-positron collider of the Budker Institute in Novosibirsk, Siberia, which reaches up to 6 GeV per beam. Its KEDR detector has measured the J/psi, psi(2S) and tau masses with record precision, using a very accurate beam-energy calibration.

summary.plain: A low-energy neutrino beam at Fermilab made by firing 8-billion-electronvolt protons at a beryllium target. It feeds the short-baseline detectors on the laboratory site.

beamline:cern-north-area.name: SPS North Area beams
beamline:cern-north-area.secondary_beam: secondary and tertiary hadron, electron and muon beams in seven beamlines serving the halls EHN1 and EHN2 and the cavern ECN3

summary.plain: The fixed-target beams of CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron: protons at 400 GeV/c strike three targets, and the secondary and tertiary beams that result feed the experiments in two surface halls and one underground cavern. It runs whenever the SPS does.

summary.plain: A beam of neutrinos sent 732 kilometres straight through the Earth's crust, from CERN in Switzerland to the Gran Sasso laboratory in Italy, between 2006 and 2012, so that the OPERA experiment could watch them change type on the way.

summary.plain: The beamline that turns J-PARC's proton beam into neutrinos: protons hit a graphite rod, magnetic "horns" focus the particles produced, and they decay in flight into neutrinos aimed slightly off to one side of the detectors 295 km away.

summary.plain: The beamline at KEK that made the world's first accelerator neutrino beam aimed at a detector hundreds of kilometres away: 12 GeV protons on an aluminium rod, two magnetic horns, and a 200-metre pipe in which the particles decayed into neutrinos.

beamline:kek-neutrino.target: Aluminium rod, 66 cm long and 3 cm in diameter, inside the first of two focusing horns

summary.plain: The facility being built at Fermilab to fire the world’s most intense beam of high-energy neutrinos 1285 kilometres through the Earth to South Dakota, plus the huge caverns that hold the detectors.

summary.plain: Fermilab’s long-running neutrino beam. Protons hit a graphite target and the particles that come out decay into neutrinos aimed at detectors in Minnesota.

beamline:numi.target: graphite target approximately 1 m in length

summary.plain: The Mainz collaboration, led by Harald Merkel, that runs the three-spectrometer electron-scattering facility A1 at MAMI.
The international collaboration of working groups from several universities that runs the A2 photoproduction experiment at MAMI.

summary.plain: The international collaboration of Mainz, Orsay, Gatchina and MIT physicists that ran the A4 parity-violation experiment at MAMI.
The MIT-based team that built and ran the ABRACADABRA-10 cm axion dark-matter search.
The scientists who built and operated the Atacama Cosmology Telescope and who still analyse its data.
The international group of scientists who run the ADMX axion dark-matter search at the University of Washington.
The Frascati, Naples, Pisa and Istituto Superiore di Sanità group that ran the Baryon-Antibaryon experiment at ADONE.
The Bologna, CERN and Frascati collaboration that ran the BCF experiment at ADONE.
The Frascati, Naples, Pavia and Rome group that ran the Boson experiment at ADONE.
The Frascati and Rome group that ran the Gamma-Gamma experiments at ADONE, first generation and, as Gamma-Gamma 2, second generation.
The Frascati, Naples, Padua and Rome group that built and ran the MEA magnetic detector at ADONE.
The Frascati, Rome and Padua group that ran the Mu-Pion experiment at ADONE.

summary.plain: The international team of scientists who run the AEgIS experiment.
The Japanese-led team of cosmic-ray physicists that built and ran the AGASA air-shower array at Akeno.
The international team of about 300 physicists who built and ran the ALEPH detector at CERN's LEP collider.

collaboration:alice.name: ALICE Collaboration

summary.plain: The international team of scientists and engineers who built and run the ALICE experiment. Formed in March 1993 when it submitted its Letter of Intent to CERN, the collaboration has grown to almost 2000 members from around 174 institutes in about 40 countries.

intervals.label: collaboration: operation (ALPHA 1 from 2005, ALPHA 2 from 2012, ALPHA-g and ALPHA 3 from 2021)

summary.plain: The international team of scientists who run the ALPHA experiment.
The DESY-based collaboration that ran ALPS I and now runs ALPS II, searching for very light, weakly interacting particles with laser light.
The collaboration running the AMBER experiment at CERN, successor to the COMPASS collaboration.

The international team (Korea, Russia, Ukraine, China, Germany and others) behind AMoRE, which searches for a hypothetical radioactive decay of molybdenum-100 using crystals cooled to a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero.
The international collaboration of physicists from the United States, Japan, China and South Korea, led by Steven Olsen of Rochester, that built and ran the AMY detector at TRISTAN.

The Spanish team at the University of Zaragoza that built and runs ANAIS-112, nine sodium-iodide crystals in the Canfranc underground laboratory, to check a long-standing claim of a yearly dark matter signal made by the DAMA experiment.
The team of scientists, led from the University of Hawai'i, who built and flew the ANITA balloon-borne neutrino detector over Antarctica five times between 2003 and 2016.
The international group of physicists who built and ran the ANNIE experiment.
The roughly 150 scientists and engineers, from institutes in about eight countries, who built and ran the ANTARES undersea neutrino telescope from 1996 until it was switched off in 2022.
The collaboration of physicists who ran the A' Experiment (APEX), a dark-photon search in Hall A at Jefferson Lab.
The team of scientists, including the group at UW-Madison's IceCube centre, who built and continue to run the ARA radio-antenna stations near the South Pole.
The team, led from ETH Zurich and CIEMAT, that built and ran the ArDM liquid argon dark matter detector, first at CERN and then in the Canfranc underground laboratory in Spain.
An Italian-Chinese collaboration of institutes of the INFN and the Chinese Academy of Sciences that built and ran ARGO-YBJ.
The international group of physicists who built and ran the ArgoNeuT experiment.
The international ARGUS collaboration that built and ran the ARGUS detector at DESY's DORIS ring and made the first observation of B-meson mixing.
The team of scientists, based at UC Irvine and partner institutions, who built and ran the now-decommissioned ARIANNA pilot neutrino experiment on the Ross Ice Shelf.

summary.plain: The international team of scientists who ran the ATHENA experiment.

The international team that built and runs the ATLAS experiment. It counts its birthday as 1 October 1992, the day it handed CERN its Letter of Intent, and today it has more than 5500 members from over 170 institutions in about 40 countries.

More than 500 scientists, engineers and graduate students from about 10 countries who built and ran the BaBar particle detector at SLAC from 1999 to 2008 to study why matter and antimatter behave differently.
The Russian-led international team of scientists building and running the Baikal-GVD neutrino telescope in Lake Baikal.

The international team of physicists who built and ran the Belle detector at the KEK laboratory in Japan and analysed its data.
The worldwide team running the Belle II experiment in Japan: more than 1100 scientists and engineers from 122 institutions in 27 countries.
The BES collaboration of the Institute of High Energy Physics and partner institutes that built and ran the first Beijing Spectrometer at BEPC.
The BES collaboration that ran the upgraded Beijing Spectrometer (BESII) at BEPC from 1998 to 2004.

summary.plain: The international BESIII collaboration of about 700 members from 86 institutions in 16 countries that built and runs the BESIII detector at the Beijing Electron-Positron Collider.

The team that has built and run the BICEP and Keck telescopes at the South Pole, searching the polarization of the Big Bang afterglow for the faint signal of gravitational waves from cosmic inflation.
The international collaboration running the BM@N experiment at the JINR Nuclotron/NICA complex.
The international team of scientists, including founders Gianpaolo Bellini and Frank Calaprice, who built and ran the Borexino solar-neutrino experiment in Italy.
The international collaboration that built and ran the BRAHMS experiment at the RHIC collider.
The group of French and other physicists who built and ran the Bugey reactor-antineutrino experiments.
The Italian, French, German, Mexican and other physicists developing BULLKID, a silicon detector array read out by superconducting sensors, and the BULLKID-DM dark matter experiment based on it.
A Japanese collaboration led from Osaka University that runs the CANDLES calcium-48 double-beta-decay experiment in the Kamioka mine.

The roughly 250 physicists and engineers from 38 institutions in five countries who built and run the SBND detector.
The international collaboration that runs the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, whose successive phases mapped the sky and, with BOSS and eBOSS, measured how fast the universe expands.
The team of physicists who built and ran the SeaQuest Drell-Yan experiment at Fermilab.
The group of physicists running the SENSEI skipper-CCD dark matter search at Fermilab.
The international team of physicists preparing the SHiP experiment at CERN.

The scientists who built and run the SND@LHC experiment at CERN.
The international team, formed in 1984 and based mainly at Queen's University, that built and ran the SNO experiment in a Canadian mine.

The physicists from Argonne, Minnesota, Oxford, Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, Tufts and Western Washington who built and ran Soudan 2.

The 609 scientists and engineers, from 55 institutions in 12 countries, who built and run the STAR heavy-ion experiment at Brookhaven's RHIC collider.

The international group of about 500 scientists from 74 institutes in Asia, Europe and the United States working on the proposed Super Tau-Charm Facility in Hefei, led by the University of Science and Technology of China.

The international team of about 560 physicists from roughly 75 institutions in 14 countries (plus CERN) who built and run the T2K experiment.
A Russian-Italian-Mongolian collaboration that runs the Tunka valley cosmic-ray and gamma-ray detectors.

The international team that built and ran the TASSO detector at DESY's PETRA collider. Centred on DESY with groups from German and British universities, the Rutherford Laboratory, the Weizmann Institute and the University of Wisconsin.
The scientists who built and run the Telescope Array cosmic-ray observatory in Utah.

The Taiwan-led collaboration, with partners in China, India and Turkey, that runs particle detectors at the Kuo-Sheng nuclear power plant in Taiwan to study neutrinos and search for very light dark matter. It was also a founding partner of China's CDEX dark matter programme.
A Japanese-Chinese collaboration that runs the Tibet air-shower array at Yangbajing.
The Japanese collaboration that built and ran the TOPAZ detector at KEK's TRISTAN collider.

The collaboration that built and ran the UA5 streamer-chamber experiment at CERN's proton-antiproton collider; John Rushbrooke was its spokesperson.

The scientists who built and run the VERITAS gamma-ray telescope array in Arizona.

The collaboration that ran the WA98 photon and hadron experiment at the CERN SPS, led first by Hans Gutbrod and from 1997 by Terry Awes.

The international team, mostly from Italian universities and INFN, with groups from Princeton and Krakow, that pioneered two-phase liquid argon detectors for WIMP dark matter at Gran Sasso with the WArP programme.
The group of institutions that built and ran the Whipple 10 m telescope in Arizona, where in 1989 the imaging Cherenkov technique first detected a TeV gamma-ray source, the Crab Nebula.

About 450 physicists who built and ran the ZEUS particle detector at DESY, in Germany, from 1992 until the HERA collider shut down in 2007.

detector:a1-mami.name: A1 spectrometers

summary.plain: Three large magnetic spectrometers, each about 15 metres long and over 200 tonnes, that measure the momentum and direction of scattered electrons and other particles with extreme precision.

detector:a1-mami.technology: Three high-resolution magnetic spectrometers about 15 m in size, each weighing more than 200 tons

detector:a2-mami.name: A2 Crystal Ball and TAPS detector system

summary.plain: The famous Crystal Ball calorimeter, a sphere of crystals around the target, combined with the TAPS wall of crystals in the forward direction and a central tracker, covering almost all directions for photons and neutral mesons.

detector:a2-mami.technology: Crystal Ball calorimeter with the TAPS forward wall and a central tracker, acceptance close to 4 pi

intervals.label: data taking (earliest documented beam time: January 2003)

detector:a4-mami.name: A4 apparatus

summary.plain: A wall of 1022 lead-fluoride crystals around the beam that counts individual scattered electrons at very high rates, together with a liquid-hydrogen target and monitors that watch the beam and target for tiny false asymmetries.

detector:a4-mami.technology: Segmented total-absorption lead-fluoride (PbF2) Cherenkov calorimeter of 1022 crystals counting individual scattered electrons; no magnetic spectrometer

detector:abracadabra.name: ABRACADABRA-10 cm apparatus

summary.plain: ABRACADABRA-10 cm was a small prototype detector at MIT that looked for a tiny magnetic signal that dark-matter axions would produce inside a toroidal magnet. It finished its axion search around 2021.

detector:abracadabra.technology: Lumped-element (broadband/resonant) toroidal magnetometer: a toroidal magnet with a SQUID-based pickup at its center senses the small oscillating magnetic field an axion dark-matter background would induce, rather than using a resonant microwave cavity.

detector:act.name: Atacama Cosmology Telescope (6 m)

summary.plain: A six-metre telescope on a 5190-metre mountain in northern Chile that mapped the faint afterglow of the Big Bang at fine detail, with successive cameras, from 2007 until it was decommissioned after taking its final data in 2022.

detector:act.technology: Six-metre off-axis Gregorian telescope feeding a cryogenic millimetre-wave bolometer camera (MBAC, then ACTPol and Advanced ACTPol receivers).

detector:admx.name: ADMX detector

summary.plain: The ADMX detector uses a powerful magnet and a supercooled tunable metal cavity to try to convert dark-matter axions into faint microwave signals, which are then amplified and measured.

detector:admx.technology: Microwave-cavity haloscope: a tunable, cylindrical copper-plated resonant cavity inside a large superconducting solenoid magnet, read out through a dilution refrigerator and a near-quantum-limited (Josephson parametric / SQUID) amplifier chain.

detector:adone-baryon-antibaryon.name: Baryon-Antibaryon (ADONE) detector

summary.plain: The Baryon-Antibaryon detector at ADONE: large liquid scintillators with wire and flash-tube chambers, built to count proton-antiproton and heavier baryon pairs near threshold.

detector:adone-baryon-antibaryon.technology: Large liquid scintillators, wire chambers with magnetostrictive reading and flash tube chambers

detector:adone-bcf.name: BCF detector

summary.plain: The BCF detector at ADONE: scintillation counters and spark chambers, carefully calibrated for particle identification.

detector:adone-bcf.technology: Scintillation counters and spark chambers with careful calibration for particle identification

detector:adone-boson.name: Boson (ADONE) detector

summary.plain: The Boson detector at ADONE: scintillators and wire chambers with magnetostrictive read-out in a compact layout covering as much solid angle as possible.

detector:adone-boson.technology: Very compact setup of scintillators and wire magnetostrictive chambers covering the maximum solid angle

detector:adone-gamma-gamma.name: Gamma-Gamma (ADONE) detector

summary.plain: The first Gamma-Gamma detector at ADONE: scintillator counters behind lead plates that convert photons, with spark chambers to show the resulting showers.

detector:adone-gamma-gamma.technology: Scintillator counters following lead plates (photon conversion) and spark chambers to show the produced showers

detector:adone-gamma-gamma-2.name: Gamma-Gamma 2 (ADONE) detector

summary.plain: The Gamma-Gamma 2 detector at ADONE: scintillation counters, converters and spark chambers covering more solid angle than its predecessor.

detector:adone-gamma-gamma-2.technology: Scintillation counters, converters and spark chambers covering a larger solid angle than the first Gamma-Gamma detector

detector:adone-mea.name: MEA detector

summary.plain: MEA at ADONE: spark chambers inside a large solenoid magnet so that the charge and momentum of every particle from an e+e- collision could be measured.

detector:adone-mea.technology: Large gap chambers and spark chambers inside a large solenoidal magnet

detector:adone-mu-pion.name: Mu-Pion (ADONE) detector

summary.plain: The Mu-Pion detector at ADONE: scintillation counters, spark chambers, water Cerenkov counters to tell pions from kaons and iron absorbers to identify muons.

detector:adone-mu-pion.technology: Scintillation counters, spark chambers read through long mirrors, water Cerenkov counters (pion/K separation), iron absorbers for muon identification and flash tube chambers

phase 2: pulsed antihydrogen source and gravity-measurement preparation

summary.plain: The AEgIS apparatus: electromagnetic traps for antiprotons and positrons, a positronium converter and lasers, with a grating deflectometer to measure how antihydrogen drops.

detector:agasa.name: AGASA surface and muon detector array

summary.plain: A field of 111 scintillator panels spread over 100 square kilometres, wired together by optical fibre to catch the particle showers of the most energetic cosmic rays.

detector:agasa.technology: Array of plastic-scintillator surface detectors on a roughly 1 km grid, linked by optical fibres, with shielded muon detectors.

detector:aleph.name: ALEPH detector

specs.calorimeters: Electromagnetic calorimeter to identify electrons and photons; hadron calorimeter to detect hadrons
specs.tracker: Silicon-microstrip vertex detector (two double-sided layers), 8-coordinate inner drift chamber with trigger, and a 4.4 m × 3.6 m time projection chamber

subsystems.description: 4.4 m long, 3.6 m in diameter, the central charged-particle tracker.
subsystems.name: Time projection chamber

subsystems.description: 6.3 m long, 5.3 m in diameter, providing a 1.5 T magnetic field.
subsystems.name: Superconducting solenoid

summary.plain: A cylindrical, general-purpose detector at LEP's Point 4, built around a giant gas chamber and a superconducting magnet to track and identify particles from electron-positron collisions.

detector:aleph.technology: General-purpose collider detector with a large-volume time projection chamber inside a superconducting solenoid

aliases: A Large Ion Collider Experiment detector

detector:alice.name: ALICE detector

specs.calorimeters: Two electromagnetic calorimeters, PHOS and EMCal
specs.muon_system: Forward muon arm (2-9 degrees polar angle): absorbers, a large dipole magnet, and fourteen planes of tracking and triggering chambers
specs.pseudorapidity_coverage: Central barrel |η| < 0.9 (TPC/TOF; TRD |η| < 0.84); forward muon spectrometer 2.5 < |η| < 4.0 (polar angle 2-9 degrees)
specs.tracker: Inner Tracking System (six planes: silicon pixel/SPD, drift/SDD, strip/SSD) plus a cylindrical Time-Projection Chamber (TPC); the TRD also contributes to tracking

subsystems: Inner Tracking System (ITS): six planes of silicon pixel (SPD), drift (SDD) and strip (SSD) detectors
Time-Projection Chamber (TPC): main tracking and dE/dx particle-identification detector
Time-of-Flight (TOF), Ring Imaging Cherenkov (HMPID) and Transition Radiation (TRD) arrays for particle identification
Forward muon spectrometer: absorbers, dipole magnet, and fourteen tracking/triggering chamber planes

summary.plain: A 10,000-tonne detector at CERN built to study collisions of lead nuclei. Layers of tracking and identification detectors sit inside a large recycled magnet, surrounded by a forward arm that catches muons, letting physicists reconstruct the thousands of particles each collision produces.

detector:alice.technology: Central barrel of silicon/gas tracking, PID and calorimetry detectors inside a solenoid magnet, plus a forward muon spectrometer

detector:alpha.name: ALPHA (ALPHA-2 and ALPHA-3 horizontal traps)

summary.plain: The horizontal ALPHA traps in which antihydrogen atoms are made, held in a magnetic bottle and illuminated with lasers and microwaves.

detector:alpha.technology: Octupole minimum-B neutral-atom trap superposed on a Penning-Malmberg trap for antihydrogen synthesis, with a catching trap and laser access (ALPHA 2/3)

detector:alpha-g.name: ALPHA-g

summary.plain: The vertical trap of the ALPHA experiment. Antihydrogen atoms are released from a magnetic trap and the detectors record whether they fall or rise, a direct test of how antimatter responds to gravity.

detector:alpha-g.technology: Vertical Penning-Malmberg and neutral-atom trap system, about double the size of ALPHA 2/3, with a precisely built, low-persistent-current magnet set

intervals.label: optical-system upgrade after the first science campaign

detector:alps-ii.name: ALPS II apparatus

summary.plain: ALPS II shines a laser at a wall to see if a tiny fraction of the light can sneak through as an undetectable particle and turn back into light on the far side, which would be a sign of new, very light particles.

detector:alps-ii.technology: Light-shining-through-a-wall apparatus: a laser beam is enhanced in a build-up optical cavity, blocked by a light-tight wall, with a second, identical regeneration cavity and superconducting dipole magnets (reused HERA magnets) on both sides, and a low-noise single-photon/heterodyne detector looking for regenerated photons on the far side.

detector:amber.name: AMBER spectrometer

summary.plain: The upgraded COMPASS spectrometer in Hall EHN2, with new liquid-hydrogen and liquid-helium targets and additional detectors for each measurement.

detector:amber.technology: Upgraded multi-purpose two-stage magnetic spectrometer (the COMPASS spectrometer) with new targets and instrumentation

detector:amore-i.name: AMoRE-I detector

summary.plain: AMoRE-I was the second stage of AMoRE: eighteen molybdate crystals (6.2 kg), cooled to about 12 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, run at the Yangyang laboratory from 2019 to 2023. It saw no sign of neutrinoless double beta decay of molybdenum-100 and set a lower limit of 2.9 x 10^24 years on its half-life.

detector:amore-i.technology: Eighteen molybdate crystals (CaMoO4 and Li2MoO4) with metallic-magnetic-calorimeter heat and light readout at mK temperatures

detector:amore-ii.name: AMoRE-II detector

summary.plain: AMoRE-II is the main, full-size stage of AMoRE, being installed at Yemilab: about 90 kg of molybdenum-100 in hundreds of lithium-molybdate crystals cooled to a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. It aims to probe the whole range of neutrino masses expected if neutrino masses follow the so-called inverted ordering.

detector:amore-ii.technology: Array of lithium-molybdate (Li2 100MoO4) scintillating crystals read out as cryogenic calorimeters with metallic magnetic calorimeters at about 10 mK

detector:amore-pilot.name: AMoRE-Pilot detector

summary.plain: AMoRE-Pilot was the first, small stage of the AMoRE experiment: six calcium-molybdate crystals (1.9 kg) cooled to a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, run at the Yangyang laboratory from 2015 to 2018 to look for neutrinoless double beta decay of molybdenum-100. It found no such decay and set a limit.

detector:amore-pilot.technology: Cryogenic calcium-molybdate scintillating crystals with metallic-magnetic-calorimeter heat and light readout at mK temperatures

summary.plain: The AMY detector at TRISTAN, built around a 3-tesla superconducting solenoid.

detector:anais-112.name: ANAIS-112 detector

summary.plain: Nine sodium iodide crystals of 12.5 kg each (112.5 kg), arranged three by three and read by photomultiplier tubes, inside a shielded hut in hall B of the Canfranc laboratory.

detector:anais-112.technology: Nine NaI(Tl) scintillator modules read by photomultiplier tubes

detector:anita.name: ANITA payload

summary.plain: A ring of radio antennas hanging beneath a giant NASA balloon, floating 37 kilometres over Antarctica and listening for the radio crackle of a neutrino hitting the ice far below.

detector:anita.technology: Balloon-borne array of quad-ridged horn antennas detecting radio-frequency Askaryan-effect pulses from neutrino- and cosmic-ray-induced showers in Antarctic ice

detector:annie-detector.name: ANNIE detector

summary.plain: A tank of gadolinium-doped water viewed by photomultiplier tubes and a few fast LAPPD light sensors, with a veto in front and an iron-scintillator muon tracker behind, in an underground hall.

detector:annie-detector.technology: Gadolinium-doped water Cherenkov detector with PMTs and LAPPD fast photodetectors and a muon range detector

detector:antares.name: ANTARES detector

summary.plain: Twelve long cables strung with light-sensing glass spheres, anchored to the Mediterranean seabed off Toulon, France. Together they watched a huge volume of seawater for the faint blue light that a neutrino leaves behind.

detector:antares.technology: Deep-sea water Cherenkov neutrino telescope: photomultiplier tubes in pressure-resistant glass spheres (optical modules) on vertical mooring lines

detector:apex-jlab.name: APEX apparatus

summary.plain: The two Hall A high-resolution spectrometers set to their smallest opening angle, with septum magnets steering electrons and positrons from a thin heavy target into them.

detector:apex-jlab.technology: Hall A High Resolution Spectrometers recording e+e- pairs from a thin high-Z target to build an invariant-mass spectrum

detector:ara.name: ARA stations

summary.plain: Five separate stations of radio antennas buried in the ice near the South Pole, each listening on its own for the radio flash of an ultra-high-energy neutrino.

detector:ara.technology: Autonomous in-ice radio (Askaryan-effect) detector stations, each an independent array of radio antennas buried 100-200 m deep in the ice

detector:ardm.name: ArDM detector

summary.plain: ArDM was a ton-scale liquid argon detector built at CERN, then installed in the Canfranc underground laboratory in the Spanish Pyrenees, to search for WIMP dark matter. It took liquid-argon data from 2015 and finished dual-phase running by about 2020. Its papers report detector performance and backgrounds, not a WIMP limit.

detector:ardm.technology: Double-phase liquid argon time projection chamber (single-phase in Run I, 2015)

detector:argo.name: ARGO detector

summary.plain: ARGO is a proposed 400-tonne liquid argon detector (300 tonnes fiducial) for the very large dark matter search planned as the last step of the Global Argon Dark Matter Collaboration. SNOLAB's Cube Hall in Canada has been selected as the prospective site. It aims to search for WIMPs down to the neutrino fog.

detector:argo.technology: Liquid argon detector (single-phase or dual-phase TPC, design open) with digital SiPM light readout

detector:argo-ybj.name: ARGO-YBJ full-coverage RPC carpet

summary.plain: A floor of particle counters, about the size of a football pitch, laid edge to edge on a Tibetan plateau to see small air showers.

detector:argo-ybj.technology: A single layer of resistive plate counters covering the whole central floor (about 78 × 74 m2) with a lead converter, read out as 18,480 pads.

physics run in the NuMI low-energy beam

detector:argoneut-detector.name: ArgoNeuT detector

summary.plain: A tank of liquid argon, 170 litres in volume, with fine wire planes that record the tracks of charged particles from neutrino interactions in three dimensions.

detector:argoneut-detector.technology: Liquid-argon time projection chamber with horizontal drift and wire-plane readout

summary.plain: The ARGUS particle detector at DESY's DORIS ring, a general-purpose detector built to study particles containing beauty and charm quarks.

detector:arianna.name: ARIANNA Hexagonal Radio Array

summary.plain: A small hexagon of radio-antenna stations that once sat on the surface of the Ross Ice Shelf, each one a self-contained listening post for neutrino signals.

detector:arianna.technology: Surface-deployed radio antenna stations detecting Askaryan-effect radio pulses from neutrino interactions in the ice below

summary.plain: The ASACUSA apparatus: a helium gas target and lasers for antiprotonic helium, and a cusp magnet that forms a beam of antihydrogen for microwave measurements.

intervals.label: data taking at the Antiproton Decelerator

summary.plain: The ATHENA trap and imaging detector, which mixed antiprotons with positrons and recorded the flashes where the resulting antihydrogen atoms annihilated.

detector:atlas.name: ATLAS detector

specs.calorimeters: Liquid-argon electromagnetic calorimeter with accordion geometry kept at -184 C, scintillator-tile hadronic calorimeter of about 420 000 tiles weighing almost 2900 tonnes, and liquid-argon hadronic end-cap and forward calorimeters
specs.muon_system: Air-core toroid muon spectrometer with three layers of precision tracking chambers - monitored drift tubes, plus resistive plate, thin-gap, small-strip thin-gap chambers and Micromegas for triggering
specs.pseudorapidity_coverage: Precision tracking |η| < 2.5; electromagnetic calorimetry |η| < 3.2 extended to |η| = 4.9 by the forward calorimeters; muon spectrometer |η| < 2.7 (trigger 2.4)
specs.tracker: Silicon pixel detector (92 million pixels, innermost layer 3.3 cm from the beam), semiconductor tracker (about 4000 modules, 6 million silicon micro-strips over 60 m²) and transition radiation tracker (300 000 thin-walled drift tubes)

subsystems.description: Pixel detector, semiconductor tracker and transition radiation tracker inside the 2 T solenoid, reconstructing charged-particle tracks and vertices for |η| < 2.5
subsystems.name: Inner Detector

subsystems.description: Accordion-geometry lead/liquid-argon sampling calorimeter measuring electron and photon energies; barrel 6.4 m long, 53 cm thick, 110 000 channels, held at -184 C
subsystems.name: Liquid-argon electromagnetic calorimeter

subsystems.description: Steel and plastic-scintillator sampling calorimeter of about 420 000 tiles and 9500 photomultipliers weighing almost 2900 tonnes, measuring hadron and jet energies in the barrel region
subsystems.name: Tile hadronic calorimeter

subsystems.description: Three layers of precision chambers in the air-core toroid field, including 1171 monitored-drift-tube chambers with 354 240 tubes, and wheels 25 m in diameter at each end
subsystems.name: Muon spectrometer

subsystems.description: Central superconducting solenoid giving 2 T in 4.5 cm of material with 38 MJ stored energy, a 25.3 m long barrel toroid of eight coils with 1.08 GJ stored, and two end-cap toroids with 0.25 GJ each
subsystems.name: Magnet system

subsystems.description: Two-stage trigger selecting interesting collisions out of up to 1.7 billion per second and writing about 1000 events per second to storage, with the first-level decision taken in under 2.5 microseconds
subsystems.name: Trigger and data acquisition

summary.plain: A cylinder 46 metres long and 25 metres across weighing 7000 tonnes - the largest particle detector ever built. Layers of tracking chambers, calorimeters and muon chambers wrap around the point where the two proton beams meet, so that almost everything produced in a collision leaves a trace somewhere.

detector:atlas.technology: General-purpose 4π collider detector with a thin superconducting solenoid around the inner-detector cavity and three large superconducting air-core toroids around the calorimeters

intervals.label: data taking at the Antiproton Decelerator
completed (true end date not published; upper bound)

summary.plain: The ATRAP traps, which hold antiprotons and positrons together and detect the antihydrogen atoms they form.

detector:babar.name: BaBar detector

summary.plain: A particle detector at SLAC built around the collision point of the PEP-II accelerator, layered so that it can pinpoint exactly where a B meson decayed and identify the particles it decayed into.

detector:babar.technology: Multi-layer silicon vertex tracker, cylindrical drift chamber, DIRC Cherenkov particle-ID detector, CsI electromagnetic calorimeter and resistive-plate-chamber muon system

detector:baikal-gvd.name: Baikal-GVD detector

summary.plain: Clusters of light-sensing spheres hanging on strings deep in Lake Baikal, added year after year since 2016, that together form a growing telescope for neutrinos from space.

detector:baikal-gvd.technology: Underwater water Cherenkov neutrino telescope: photomultiplier-equipped optical modules on vertical strings organised into clusters

detector:baksan-underground-scintillatio.name: Baksan Underground Scintillation Telescope detector

summary.plain: A tall block of 3,184 scintillator tanks, stacked in planes, that records the track and timing of every particle passing through.

detector:baksan-underground-scintillatio.technology: Four-storey building of liquid-scintillator counters (aluminium tanks, white-spirit scintillator, one photomultiplier each): four horizontal and four vertical planes, 3184 counters, 330 t of scintillator

intervals.label: antiproton runs at the Antiproton Decelerator

detector:base.name: BASE multi-Penning-trap system

summary.plain: Four connected electromagnetic traps held at very low temperature. One stores antiprotons for months, one identifies a single antiproton’s spin, one measures it precisely and one cools it.

detector:base.technology: Cryogenic multi-Penning-trap system with analysis, precision, cooling and reservoir traps

detector:belle.name: Belle detector

summary.plain: The large barrel-shaped particle detector that surrounded the collision point of the KEKB machine from 1999 to 2010. A powerful magnet bent the tracks of the particles produced so that their momenta could be measured.

detector:belle.technology: general-purpose 4π magnetic spectrometer built around a 1.5 T superconducting solenoid

detector:belle-ii.name: Belle II detector

subsystems.description: Two layers of pixelated silicon sensors immediately around the beam pipe, measuring decay-vertex positions. A new, fully implemented pixel detector was installed during Long Shutdown 1.
subsystems.name: PXD — pixel vertex detector

subsystems.description: Four layers of double-sided silicon strip sensors surrounding the PXD.
subsystems.name: SVD — silicon vertex detector

subsystems.description: The main tracking device: a large gas volume strung with sense and field wires that measures charged-particle trajectories, momenta and specific ionisation (dE/dx).
subsystems.name: CDC — central drift chamber

subsystems.description: A barrel-shaped array of quartz-radiator Cherenkov counters used for charged-hadron identification.
subsystems.name: TOP — time-of-propagation counters

subsystems.description: A ring-imaging Cherenkov counter with an aerogel radiator in the forward end-cap, complementing the TOP for particle identification.
subsystems.name: ARICH — aerogel ring-imaging Cherenkov counter

subsystems.description: Scintillator crystals inside the solenoid that measure the energies of photons and electrons.
subsystems.name: ECL — electromagnetic calorimeter

subsystems.description: The instrumented iron flux return outside the solenoid, which detects long-lived neutral kaons and identifies muons.
subsystems.name: KLM — K-long and muon detector

summary.plain: The detector that records what comes out of the SuperKEKB collisions. Seven layers of instruments, wrapped in a strong magnet, track and identify the particles produced when electrons and positrons annihilate.

detector:belle-ii.technology: general-purpose 4π magnetic spectrometer with seven subdetectors inside a 1.5 T superconducting solenoid

detector:bes.name: BES detector

summary.plain: The first Beijing Spectrometer: a drift-chamber and streamer-tube calorimeter detector around the collision point of BEPC, designed to measure charged particles and photons in the tau-charm energy region.

detector:bes.technology: Central drift chamber (CDC) inside a main drift chamber (MDC) with an electromagnetic calorimeter of self-quenching streamer tubes interleaved with lead

detector:bes-ii.name: BES-II detector

summary.plain: The upgraded Beijing Spectrometer: BESI with a new vertex detector, main drift chamber and barrel time-of-flight system.

detector:bes-ii.technology: BESI upgraded with a revamped MARK II vertex detector in place of the central drift chamber and a new main drift chamber and barrel time-of-flight system

intervals.label: commissioning with the first BEPCII collisions

detector:bes-iii.name: BES-III detector

summary.plain: The BESIII detector: a layered cylinder around the collision point with a helium drift chamber, scintillator timing counters, a crystal calorimeter and muon counters inside a 1-tesla superconducting magnet, covering 93% of all directions.

detector:bes-iii.technology: Helium-based multilayer drift chamber, plastic-scintillator TOF and CsI(Tl) electromagnetic calorimeter inside a 1.0 T superconducting solenoid, with resistive-plate-chamber muon identifier

detector:bicep-array.name: BICEP Array

summary.plain: The newest BICEP/Keck instrument: four 55-centimetre refracting telescopes covering six frequency bands from 30 to 270 GHz, built to separate galactic dust and synchrotron from a possible inflationary signal.

detector:bicep-array.technology: Four 550 mm aperture refracting telescopes (receivers) observing CMB polarization at 30/40, 95, 150 and 220/270 GHz.

detector:bicep1.name: BICEP1 telescope

summary.plain: A small two-lens refracting telescope looking out through the roof of a laboratory near the South Pole, built to look for the faint polarization pattern that gravitational waves from inflation would leave in the Big Bang afterglow.

detector:bicep1.technology: Two-lens refracting telescope with a focal plane of 49 orthogonal pairs of horn-coupled polarization-sensitive bolometers at 100 and 150 GHz.

detector:bicep2.name: BICEP2 telescope

summary.plain: A 26-centimetre refracting telescope with 512 superconducting detectors that observed a patch of the southern sky from the South Pole for three seasons.

detector:bicep2.technology: All-cold refracting optical system, 26 cm aperture, with a focal plane of 512 antenna-coupled transition edge sensor 150 GHz bolometers.

detector:bicep3.name: BICEP3 telescope

summary.plain: A 52-centimetre refracting telescope in the Dark Sector Laboratory at the South Pole with 2560 superconducting detectors at 95 GHz, the most sensitive BICEP/Keck instrument at that frequency.

detector:bicep3.technology: Compact two-lens refracting telescope, 520 mm aperture, 95 GHz, with modular antenna-coupled TES focal-plane tiles.

detector:bmn.name: BM@N spectrometer

summary.plain: A forward magnetic spectrometer with a large dipole magnet, silicon and gas tracking, time-of-flight and calorimeters that records the particles produced when heavy ions hit a fixed target.

detector:bmn.technology: Forward magnetic spectrometer with a dipole magnet, beam monitoring, tracking, time-of-flight and calorimeters

detector:borexino.name: Borexino detector

summary.plain: A nylon sphere full of ultra-pure liquid, watched by photomultiplier tubes, that catches the faint flashes of light neutrinos leave behind as they pass through.

detector:borexino.technology: A nylon-sphere vessel of pseudocumene+PPO liquid scintillator viewed by photomultiplier tubes, surrounded by buffer liquid and a water-Cherenkov muon veto

detector:boss-spectrographs.name: BOSS spectrographs

summary.plain: Two identical fibre-fed spectrographs, rebuilt from the original SDSS ones, that record the colours of up to 1,000 galaxies or quasars at once for BOSS, eBOSS and now SDSS-V.

detector:boss-spectrographs.technology: Two identical dual-channel fibre-fed optical spectrographs rebuilt from the original SDSS spectrographs, fed by 1,000 fibres in 3-degree plug plates for BOSS and eBOSS.

detector:brahms.name: BRAHMS spectrometers

summary.plain: Two movable particle spectrometers that could be swung to different angles around the collision point to catch charged particles over a wide range of directions and momenta.

detector:brahms.technology: Movable magnetic spectrometers measuring identified charged hadrons over a wide range of rapidity and transverse momentum

intervals.label: Bugey-4 and Bugey-3 measurements (dates of data taking not found)

detector:bugey-detector.name: Bugey-3 detectors

summary.plain: Three identical tanks of liquid scintillator, each split into 98 cells, placed at 15, 40 and 95 metres from a reactor core so their antineutrino spectra could be compared.

detector:bugey-detector.technology: Segmented 6Li-loaded (0.15 %) liquid-scintillator detectors, 98 cells each, with pulse-shape discrimination

intervals.label: planned installation of the 3-detector demonstrator at the LNGS cryo-platform
planned installation of the final experiment at the LNGS cryo-platform

detector:bullkid-dm.name: BULLKID-DM silicon-dice KID array

summary.plain: A stack of thin silicon wafers, each carved into hundreds of tiny blocks, with a superconducting sensor on each wafer that notices the heat of a particle hitting any block.

detector:bullkid-dm.technology: Diced silicon wafers read out by multiplexed phonon-mediated kinetic inductance detectors

detector:c-4.name: C-4 detector array

summary.plain: C-4 was designed as a bigger version of CoGeNT: four germanium detectors, each about three times heavier, in a better-shielded setup in the Soudan mine, to test CoGeNT's low-energy excess. Only the design paper was read; no result or start of data taking was found.

detector:c-4.technology: Four p-type point-contact germanium crystals in a common low-background shield (proposed)

detector:candles-detector.name: CANDLES III detector

summary.plain: A tank of liquid scintillator holding 96 cubes of calcium fluoride crystal, watched by 62 photomultiplier tubes. The liquid vetoes radiation from outside while the crystals both host the decay and flash when it happens.

detector:candles-detector.technology: CaF2 scintillating crystals with wavelength-shifter layers, immersed in a liquid scintillator that acts as a 4pi active shield, read out by photomultiplier tubes

detector:cangaroo-iii.name: CANGAROO-III telescope array

summary.plain: Four 10 metre telescopes standing at the corners of a diamond in the Australian outback, each with a camera that photographs the flash of light from a gamma-ray air shower.

detector:cangaroo-iii.technology: Four 10 m imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes, each a parabolic reflector of 114 small spherical FRP mirrors of 80 cm diameter.

detector:cast.name: CAST detector

summary.plain: The CAST detector reused a retired magnet originally built for the Large Hadron Collider, pointed it at the Sun, and looked for the faint X-rays that would appear if hypothetical axion particles convert into light inside the magnet.

detector:cast.technology: Axion helioscope: a decommissioned LHC prototype superconducting dipole magnet, pointed at the Sun, with its hollow beam-pipe bores acting as viewing tubes for X-ray optics and X-ray detectors that look for photons produced by solar axions converting in the magnetic field.

intervals.label: construction of the experiment at the FAIR site

detector:cbm.name: CBM detector (planned)

summary.plain: A set of fast, radiation-hard detectors in a magnet that will track and identify particles from heavy-ion collisions at up to ten million interactions per second.

detector:cbm.technology: Free-streaming, self-triggered readout with radiation-hard, low-mass detectors for vertexing, tracking, particle identification and event characterisation

intervals.label: completed (CCFR data taking; detector continued as NuTeV)

detector:ccfr-detector.name: CCFR Lab E neutrino detector

summary.plain: A 690-tonne wall of steel plates interleaved with plastic scintillator and tracking chambers, followed by a magnetised iron muon spectrometer, in Lab E at Fermilab.

detector:ccfr-detector.technology: 690 t steel-scintillator target calorimeter with drift chambers followed by an iron toroidal muon spectrometer

detector:ccm-detector.name: Coherent CAPTAIN-Mills detector (CCM120 / CCM200)

summary.plain: The CCM detector: a steel tank of liquid argon with 200 light sensors, built to see the faint flashes made when a neutrino or a dark-matter particle nudges an argon nucleus.

detector:ccm-detector.technology: Single-phase liquid-argon light-collection detector (scintillation and Cherenkov light, no drift field or charge readout); 80 % of the PMTs coated with a wavelength shifter, 20 % uncoated

detector:cdex-1.name: CDEX-1 detector

summary.plain: CDEX-1 was the first stage of the CDEX programme: a single 1 kg germanium crystal in the Jinping underground laboratory in China, tuned to notice the tiny energy of very light dark matter particles. It saw no dark matter, and its results disfavoured earlier claimed signals.

detector:cdex-1.technology: p-type point-contact germanium detector (994 g crystal) with sub-keV threshold

detector:cdex-10.name: CDEX-10 detector

summary.plain: CDEX-10 is the second stage of the CDEX programme: ten kilograms of germanium crystals bathed in liquid nitrogen in the Jinping underground laboratory in China. It searches for very light dark matter and has set limits down to a few MeV.

detector:cdex-10.technology: Array of p-type point-contact germanium detectors immersed in liquid nitrogen

detector:cdex-50.name: CDEX-50 detector

summary.plain: CDEX-50 is a proposed next stage of the CDEX programme: 50 kilograms of germanium detectors bathed in liquid nitrogen in the expanded Jinping underground laboratory in China, aimed at very light dark matter.

detector:cdex-50.technology: Array of 50 kg of p-type point-contact germanium detectors in a liquid-nitrogen tank (proposed)

detector:cdf.name: CDF detector

specs.calorimeters: 23 layers of lead and scintillating plastic (electromagnetic) and 23 layers of steel and scintillating plastic (hadronic) sampling calorimeters
specs.muon_system: Outer layer of muon drift chambers catching muons that pass through the calorimeters
specs.tracker: 7 layers of silicon microstrip detectors around the beam pipe plus a large open-cell drift ("wire") chamber recording up to 96 position measurements per particle

summary.plain: A four-story-tall, roughly 4,500-tonne particle detector built around the point where Fermilab's Tevatron collided protons with antiprotons, used to trace and measure the particles produced.

detector:cdf.technology: General-purpose solenoidal collider detector with silicon and drift-chamber tracking, sampling calorimetry and muon chambers

detector:cdhs-detector.name: CDHS detector

summary.plain: A stack of magnetised iron slabs with tracking chambers between them: neutrinos strike the iron, and the chambers follow the muon and the hadron shower that come out.

detector:cdhs-detector.technology: Magnetised iron modules separated by wire drift chambers, serving as muon spectrometer and hadron calorimeter

intervals.label: WIMP-search data runs at the Stanford Underground Facility

detector:cdms-i.name: CDMS I detectors

summary.plain: The first stage of the Cryogenic Dark Matter Search: germanium and silicon crystals cooled to 20 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, in a shallow tunnel under Stanford University. Its 2000 result excluded, at more than 84% confidence, the whole dark matter signal region reported by the DAMA experiment.

detector:cdms-i.technology: Cryogenic Ge (BLIP) and Si (ZIP) detectors measuring phonons and ionization simultaneously

detector:cdms-ii.name: CDMS II detector

description: Five towers, each containing six detectors (disks ~10 mm thick, 76 mm in diameter)
subsystems.name: Towers

summary.plain: Thirty disk-shaped crystals of germanium and silicon, each about the size of a hockey puck, cooled to below one-twentieth of a degree above absolute zero to catch the faint recoil of a dark matter particle hitting an atom.

detector:cdms-ii.technology: Cryogenic germanium and silicon detectors reading both ionization and phonon (heat) signals from particle recoils, arranged in towers

summary.plain: The CELLO particle detector at DESY's PETRA ring, installed in 1980 in the collision region previously used by PLUTO.

detector:charm-detector.name: CHARM detector

summary.plain: A low-density calorimeter of marble plates and tracking tubes, chosen so that neutrino collisions would leave clear, easily measured tracks, with a muon spectrometer behind it.

detector:charm-detector.technology: Low-density, low-Z calorimeter of marble plates interspersed with planes of proportional tubes and scintillators, followed by a muon spectrometer with magnetised iron toroids

detector:charm-ii-detector.name: CHARM II detector

summary.plain: A very large, fine-grained calorimeter made of glass plates and tracking planes, with a magnet behind it, designed so that a neutrino scattering off a single electron could be seen.

detector:charm-ii-detector.technology: Massive fine-grained low-density calorimeter with a glass target, followed by a magnetic spectrometer

detector:chooz-detector.name: CHOOZ detector

summary.plain: A tank of liquid scintillator doped with gadolinium and viewed by photomultiplier tubes, placed in a tunnel under a hill about a kilometre from the reactors.

detector:chooz-detector.technology: Gd-loaded paraffin-based liquid scintillator target with surrounding unloaded scintillator regions and PMTs

intervals.label: first operation (CERN Courier: began operation in 1993)

detector:chorus-detector.name: CHORUS detector

summary.plain: A block of nuclear emulsion, fine-grained enough to show the tiny kink of a decaying tau lepton, backed by electronic trackers, calorimeters and a muon spectrometer that tell where in the emulsion to look.

detector:chorus-detector.technology: Hybrid detector: nuclear-emulsion target with trigger hodoscopes, scintillating-fibre trackers, a hadron spectrometer, electromagnetic and hadronic calorimeters and a muon spectrometer

detector:clas.name: CLAS detector
subsystems: Six-coil superconducting toroidal magnet providing a largely azimuthal field

summary.plain: A large, six-sector particle detector built around a toroidal magnet, surrounding the target in Hall B so it could follow almost every particle produced when an electron or photon hit a nucleus.

detector:clas.technology: Large-acceptance toroidal-field magnetic spectrometer with drift chambers, Cherenkov counters, time-of-flight scintillators and electromagnetic calorimeters

detector:clas12.name: CLAS12 detector
subsystems: Superconducting torus magnet covering forward polar angles up to 35 degrees; solenoid magnet and detector covering 35 to 125 degrees

summary.plain: A large detector with two magnets that surrounds the target in Hall B and tracks almost every charged and neutral particle produced when the 12 GeV electron beam strikes a target.

detector:clas12.technology: Dual-magnet large-acceptance spectrometer: superconducting torus with drift chambers (forward) and solenoid with vertex tracker (central), plus Cherenkov counters, time-of-flight scintillators and electromagnetic calorimeters

detector:class.name: CLASS telescope array

summary.plain: An array of four microwave telescopes in the Chilean Andes that scan most of the sky with a rapidly spinning polarization modulator to measure the largest-scale polarization of the Big Bang afterglow.

detector:class.technology: Array of four microwave telescopes with front-end polarization modulators and TES bolometers at 40, 90, 150 and 220 GHz.

detector:cleo.name: CLEO detector

summary.plain: The CLEO particle detector at Cornell's CESR ring. A magnetic solenoid detector that was rebuilt and upgraded five times over thirty years with new trackers, calorimeters, particle-identification systems and silicon vertex detectors.

detector:cleo.technology: Magnetic spectrometer detector with a drift-chamber tracker, a calorimeter, particle-identification systems and, from 1995, a silicon vertex detector; upgraded five times

detector:cmb-s4.name: CMB-S4 telescopes (proposed)

summary.plain: A planned set of large and small microwave telescopes at the South Pole and in Chile, meant to detect primordial gravitational waves. In July 2025 the US DOE and NSF said they could no longer support the project.

detector:cmb-s4.technology: Large and small aperture telescopes with predominantly dichroic detectors covering 11 observing bands.

summary.plain: The CMD-1 detector, first of the Cryogenic Magnetic Detector line at VEPP-2M in Novosibirsk.
The CMD-2 detector: the second Cryogenic Magnetic Detector, built at the Budker Institute for the VEPP-2M collider.

detector:cmd-3.name: CMD-3 detector

summary.plain: The CMD-3 detector: a superconducting solenoid around the collision point with a drift chamber, time-of-flight counters, three types of calorimeter and muon counters, measuring the products of electron-positron collisions at up to 2 GeV.

detector:cmd-3.technology: Magnetic detector with a drift chamber, time-of-flight counters, an electromagnetic calorimeter of liquid xenon, CsI and BGO and muon counters in a 1.0-1.3 T field

detector:cms.name: CMS detector

specs.calorimeters: lead-tungstate (PbWO4) scintillating-crystal electromagnetic calorimeter and brass-scintillator sampling hadron calorimeter, with forward sampling calorimeters
specs.muon_system: four stations of muon detectors instrumenting the iron flux-return yoke: drift tubes and resistive plate chambers in the barrel, cathode strip chambers, resistive plate chambers and GEM chambers in the endcaps

subsystems.description: The largest superconducting magnet ever built; its coils and iron return yoke dominate the detector mass and the yoke is 14 m in diameter.
subsystems.name: Superconducting solenoid

subsystems.description: All-silicon pixel and strip tracker covering an area the size of a tennis court with 135 million readout channels and ~10 µm single-point accuracy.
subsystems.name: Silicon tracker

subsystems.description: Lead-tungstate (PbWO4) scintillating crystals that stop electrons and photons and measure their energy.
subsystems.name: Electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL)

subsystems.description: Brass and scintillator sampling calorimeter that stops hadrons passing through the ECAL.
subsystems.name: Hadron calorimeter (HCAL)

subsystems.description: 1400 muon chambers embedded in the steel return yoke: drift tubes, cathode strip chambers, resistive plate chambers and GEM chambers.
subsystems.name: Muon system

subsystems.description: A two-level trigger reduces the 40 MHz bunch-crossing rate to about 100 kHz at Level-1 and to about 100 events per second after the High-Level Trigger.
subsystems.name: Trigger and data acquisition

summary.plain: A 21-metre-long, 14 000-tonne particle detector wrapped around one of the points where the Large Hadron Collider's proton beams cross. Its huge magnet bends the paths of the particles produced so that their momenta can be measured.

detector:cms.technology: general-purpose 4π collider detector built around a 3.8 T superconducting solenoid, with an all-silicon tracker, a lead-tungstate crystal electromagnetic calorimeter, a brass/scintillator sampling hadron calorimeter and muon detectors in the iron flux-return yoke

intervals.label: underground installation and cooldown at Soudan
initial run (442 live days to 6 March 2011)
outage after the Soudan access-shaft fire
continuous data taking after the fire (data set analysed to 23 April 2013)

detector:cogent.name: CoGeNT detector

summary.plain: CoGeNT ran a single 440-gram germanium crystal in the Soudan mine in Minnesota to look for very light dark matter. It reported an unexplained excess of low-energy events and a seasonal rate change that fit light dark matter, but called their origin unknown and the significance low, and other experiments did not confirm them.

detector:cogent.technology: Single modified BEGe p-type point-contact (PPC) germanium diode with sub-keV threshold

summary.plain: A 22-kilogram tank of liquid argon that made the first measurement of coherent neutrino scattering off argon nuclei, a step toward the argon detectors used by much larger neutrino and dark-matter experiments.
A 14.6-kilogram crystal of caesium iodide that made the first direct observation of coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, a process predicted for decades but never before caught.

intervals.label: Ge-Mini operation, evidence of CEvNS on germanium

detector:coherent-ge.name: COHERENT germanium array (Ge-Mini)

summary.plain: An array of eight ultra-pure germanium crystals, together weighing about 17.6 kilograms, that in 2024 became the third type of atomic nucleus on which COHERENT caught neutrinos bouncing off gently.

detector:coherent-ge.technology: array of high-purity, p-type point-contact (inverted-coaxial) germanium spectrometers

summary.plain: A 185-kilogram sodium-iodide detector used to measure background rates and study how neutrinos interact with iodine, a step toward a much larger planned sodium-iodide detector.

detector:comet.name: COMET detector

summary.plain: A curved tunnel of superconducting magnets at the J-PARC laboratory in Japan that bends and slows down muons, feeding them into a detector built to catch the single electron that would appear if a muon converted into one.

detector:comet.technology: Curved superconducting solenoid pion/muon transport (capture and transport solenoids) feeding a detector solenoid instrumented with cylindrical drift chamber and trigger hodoscope (CyDet, Phase-I) or straw tracker and electromagnetic calorimeter (StrECAL)

detector:compass.name: COMPASS spectrometer

summary.plain: A two-stage magnetic spectrometer with a large polarised target, tracking chambers, a ring-imaging Cherenkov counter and calorimeters, built to follow all particles from beam collisions with a target.

detector:compass.technology: Two-stage, large-angle and large-momentum-range magnetic spectrometer with polarised target, RICH and calorimeters

intervals.label: engineering run with a 4 g prototype
data taking with the upgraded CCD array

detector:connie-detector.name: CONNIE CCD array

summary.plain: A cooled array of silicon camera sensors, so quiet that a single nuclear recoil of about a thousand electronvolts shows up, inside a thick lead and polyethylene shield.

detector:connie-detector.technology: Array of low-noise fully depleted charge-coupled devices (CCDs) operated cryogenically

target_mass.display: 4 kg (4 × 1 kg) nominal; 2.83 ± 0.02 kg active at Leibstadt

summary.plain: Four one-kilogram blocks of ultra-pure germanium, first used at a German nuclear plant and later moved to a Swiss one, sensitive enough to feel the tiny nudge of a reactor antineutrino bouncing off a whole atomic nucleus.

intervals.label: detector assembly at Y2L (early 2016) and commissioning
physics data taking at Y2L (6.4 years)

detector:cosine-100.name: COSINE-100 detector

summary.plain: COSINE-100 was a 106 kg array of eight sodium-iodide crystals at the Yangyang underground laboratory, built to test the long-disputed claim by the DAMA experiment of a yearly rise and fall in dark-matter-like signals, using the same kind of crystal. It ran from 2016 to 2023 and has not confirmed the DAMA signal.

detector:cosine-100.technology: Array of eight low-background NaI(Tl) crystals read by photomultiplier tubes inside a liquid-scintillator veto

intervals.label: decommissioning at Y2L, relocation, upgrade and installation at Yemilab
physics data taking at the nominal -30 C

detector:cosine-100u.name: COSINE-100U detector

summary.plain: COSINE-100U is the upgraded COSINE-100 experiment: the same eight sodium-iodide crystals, moved to the deeper Yemilab laboratory and re-fitted so that more of their light is collected. It aims to look for lighter dark matter and has been taking data there since September 2025.

detector:cosine-100u.technology: Eight NaI(Tl) crystals with photomultiplier tubes coupled directly to the crystal end faces, in a liquid-scintillator veto in a -30 C room

intervals.label: R&D project and proposed NaI cryogenic calorimeter at LNGS
construction of the experimental facility at LNGS
underground run of a 3.67 g NaI remoTES prototype at LNGS
commissioning of the cryostat and facility; first physics run (COSINUS-1pi Run1) awaited
